seoDescription: Learn how to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) in your generative AI applications using MLflow and DagsHub. This tutorial demonstrates setting up an MLflow experiment to track and assess the performance of a GPT-4 model from OpenAI. Discover how to use MLflow's `evaluate` function with custom metrics like toxicity, latency, and answer similarity, and compare generated outputs against ground truth data. Finally, see how to integrate DagsHub to remotely log, visualize, and compare your LLM evaluation results.

chapters.title: Introduction to MLflow for Generative AI
chapters.description: This chapter introduces MLflow as a tool for managing machine learning projects and explains how it can be applied to generative AI and LLM evaluation, including integration with DagsHub.

chapters.title: Exploring MLflow's Capabilities and the Project Goal
chapters.description: This section covers the core features of MLflow, such as the tracking server, and outlines the video's focus on using it to evaluate and track LLM applications.

chapters.title: Project Environment and Library Setup
chapters.description: A walkthrough of the initial notebook setup, detailing the necessary Python libraries like MLflow, OpenCV, Pandas, and DagsHub.

chapters.title: Preparing the Test Dataset
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to construct a test dataset using a Pandas DataFrame, including 'inputs' for questions and 'ground_truth' for the expected answers.

chapters.title: Configuring the MLflow Experiment with GPT-4
chapters.description: This part details setting up and starting an MLflow experiment, wrapping the GPT-4 model using `mlflow.openai.log_model`, and defining the system and user prompts.

chapters.title: Applying Predefined Evaluation Metrics
chapters.description: A look into the MLflow documentation for supported LLM evaluation metrics and how to use `mlflow.evaluate` with custom metrics like toxicity, latency, and answer similarity.

chapters.title: Running the Local Experiment and Analyzing Results
chapters.description: This chapter covers executing the Python script to run the local MLflow experiment, setting the OpenAI API key, and then analyzing the generated `eval.csv` file to understand the results.

chapters.title: Integrating DagsHub for Remote Experiment Tracking
chapters.description: This section explains how to push the experiment results to a remote DagsHub server by setting up the DagsHub repository and configuring the tracking URI in the code.

chapters.title: Visualizing and Comparing Experiments in DagsHub
chapters.description: The final chapter showcases the DagsHub UI, demonstrating how to view logged metrics and use the integrated MLflow UI to compare different experiment runs side-by-side with charts.

summary:
## Core Concepts

*   **MLflow for Generative AI:** Use MLflow to manage the full lifecycle of Large Language Model (LLM) applications. This includes experiment tracking, model logging, and robust performance evaluation.
*   **DagsHub Integration:** Leverage DagsHub as a remote, collaborative backend for MLflow. It allows you to store, visualize, and compare your LLM experiments in a central, shareable location.

## Project Workflow

1.  **Setup:** Install the required libraries: `mlflow`, `openai`, `dagshub`, and `pandas`.
2.  **Data Preparation:** Create a `pandas.DataFrame` containing `inputs` (prompts/questions) and a `ground_truth` column with the ideal answers for comparison.
3.  **Model Logging:** Wrap a generative model, such as OpenAI's GPT-4, as an MLflow model. This is done using `mlflow.openai.log_model()`, where you define the task (e.g., `chat.completion`) and the default message structure.
4.  **Evaluation:** Use the powerful `mlflow.evaluate()` function to assess the model's performance against the ground truth data using various metrics.
5.  **Remote Tracking:** Configure your script to point to a DagsHub repository. This pushes all experiment parameters, metrics, and artifacts to the remote server automatically.

> [!TIP]
> To run the code, you need to set your OpenAI API key as an environment variable:
> `export OPENAI_API_KEY='your-key-here'`

## Key Functions & Configuration

*   **`mlflow.openai.log_model()`**: This function registers the LLM with MLflow, making it a trackable artifact.
    ```python
    logged_model_info = mlflow.openai.log_model(
        model="gpt-4",
        task="openai.chat.completion",
        artifact_path="model",
        messages=[...]
    )
    ```

*   **`mlflow.evaluate()`**: The core function for running the evaluation.
    > [!IMPORTANT]
    > Key parameters for `mlflow.evaluate()` include:
    > *   `model`: The URI of the logged model (e.g., `logged_model_info.model_uri`).
    > *   `data`: The input `DataFrame` for testing.
    > *   `targets`: The column name containing the ground truth answers.
    > *   `model_type`: The task type, such as `"question-answering"`.
    > *   `extra_metrics`: A list of additional metrics to compute beyond the defaults.

*   **DagsHub Configuration**: To enable remote logging, initialize DagsHub and set the MLflow tracking URI.
    ```python
    import dagshub
    import mlflow

    dagshub.init(repo_owner='OWNER', repo_name='REPO_NAME', mlflow=True)
    mlflow.set_tracking_uri('https://dagshub.com/OWNER/REPO_NAME.mlflow')
    ```

## Evaluation Metrics for LLMs

MLflow supports several built-in and extra metrics for evaluating LLMs, especially for `question-answering` tasks:

*   **Readability Scores:**
    *   `ari_grade_level`: Automated Readability Index.
    *   `flesch_kincaid_grade_level`: Indicates the required education level to understand the text.
*   **GenAI-Based Metrics:**
    *   `answer_similarity`: Uses a separate AI model to score the semantic similarity between the generated output and the ground truth.
*   **Performance & Safety Metrics:**
    *   `latency`: Measures the time taken to generate a response.
    *   `toxicity`: Assesses the presence of toxic content in the output.
